name: Python Basics
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Run Python scripts and the REPL, then use types, strings, input, if, loops, lists and functions, and read errors.

lesson.intro: Python is the most popular first language for good reasons: it reads almost like English, and you can run a line the moment you write it. This lesson takes you from running your first script to writing small programs with numbers, text, decisions, loops, lists and functions. Just as important, you will learn to read the error messages Python gives you, because every programmer sees them every day.
objectives: Run a Python script from the terminal and use the REPL to try ideas quickly
Predict the output of short programs that use arithmetic, strings, if, for, while and lists
Convert user input to numbers and format output with f-strings
Write small functions that take parameters and return values
Read a traceback to find the error type, the message and the line that failed

sections.title: Running Python: scripts and the REPL
sections.body:
You write `print("Hello, Recurse!")` in a file called `hello.py`, open a terminal in that folder and type `python3 hello.py`. Python reads the file, runs it and prints the greeting. That file is a **script**: a text file of Python code that runs from top to bottom and then exits. (On Windows the command is usually `python` or `py` instead of `python3`.)

Type `python3` on its own and you get the **REPL** instead (read, evaluate, print, loop), with a `>>>` prompt. Each line runs as soon as you press Enter, and the REPL echoes the value of any expression you type, so `2 + 3` shows `5` without a print. That echo only happens in the REPL. In a script, a bare `2 + 3` is calculated and thrown away, so you must `print()` whatever you want to see. Use the REPL to try one idea quickly and a script for anything you want to keep. Leave the REPL with `exit()` or Ctrl+D (Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows).

Python runs a script one **statement** at a time, starting at the first line and moving down. A variable only exists after the line that assigns it has run, and assigning to it again replaces the old value. Lines starting with `#` are comments: Python ignores them, and you use them to explain why the code does something.

Indentation is part of the syntax. The indented lines under an `if`, `for` or `def` form a block, and the block ends where the indentation goes back. Use four spaces per level and let your editor insert them.

Two kinds of errors stop a program:
- A **syntax error**, such as a missing colon or an unclosed quote, is found before anything runs, because Python checks the whole file first. No output appears at all.
- A **runtime error**, such as using a name that doesn't exist, stops the program at that line. Everything above it has already run.
sections.code:
$ python3 hello.py
Hello, Recurse!
$ python3
>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> name = "Ada"
>>> name
'Ada'
>>> print(name)
Ada
>>> exit()
$
sections.tip: Keep a REPL open next to your editor. When you are unsure what an expression does, type it in and look instead of guessing.
sections.pitfall: Typing `python3 hello.py` at the `>>>` prompt gives a SyntaxError. That command belongs in the terminal, not inside the REPL, so type `exit()` first.

check.question: A script prints start, then a line uses a misspelled variable name, then a line prints end. What do you see?
choices: Only the error, because Python checks every name before running
start and end, then the error
Nothing, because the file is rejected before it runs
check.explanation: A misspelled name is a runtime error (NameError), so Python only discovers it when it reaches that line. start has already printed and end never runs. Only syntax errors stop a file before anything runs.

sections.title: Values, types and arithmetic
sections.body:
A recipe needs 250 grams of flour per batch and you want 3 batches: `250 * 3` is 750. You need 7 eggs and they come in boxes of 6: `7 // 6` is 1 full box, and `7 % 6` says 1 egg is left over. A lot of everyday programming is arithmetic like this.

Every value in Python has a **type**, which decides what you can do with it. The four you meet first:
- `int`: whole numbers such as `42`, `-7` and `0`.
- `float`: numbers with a decimal point such as `3.14` and `2.0`.
- `str`: text in quotes such as `"hello"` or `'42'`. The quotes make it text, so `'42'` is not a number.
- `bool`: `True` or `False`, with capital letters.

`type(value)` tells you the type of anything, which is handy in the REPL when a result surprises you.

The arithmetic operators are `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` (division), `//` (**floor division**: divide and round down), `%` (**modulo**: the remainder) and `**` (power). Two details catch everyone at first:
- `/` always gives a float, even when the division is exact: `10 / 2` is `5.0`.
- `//` rounds down toward negative infinity, not toward zero: `7 // 2` is `3` but `-7 // 2` is `-4`.

`//` and `%` work as a pair. `n % 2 == 0` tests whether n is even, `n % 10` gives the last digit, and `minutes // 60` with `minutes % 60` splits a number of minutes into hours and minutes.

Python follows the usual math order: `**` first, then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%`, then `+` and `-`. Operators at the same level run left to right. When in doubt, add parentheses: they cost nothing and make your intent obvious to the next reader.

Mixing an int and a float gives a float (`2 + 0.5` is `2.5`). Floats are stored in binary, so some decimals come out slightly off: `0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.30000000000000004`. That happens in every language, and the Variables and Types topic explains why.
sections.code:
print(type(42))      # <class 'int'>
print(type("42"))    # <class 'str'>
print(10 / 2)        # 5.0  (/ always gives a float)
print(7 // 2)        # 3    (floor division)
print(7 % 2)         # 1    (remainder, so 7 is odd)
print(-7 // 2)       # -4   (rounds down, not toward zero)
print(2 ** 10)       # 1024
print(2 + 3 * 4)     # 14
print((2 + 3) * 4)   # 20

minutes = 135
print(minutes // 60, "h", minutes % 60, "min")   # 2 h 15 min
sections.pitfall: Expecting `/` to give a whole number. `9 / 3` is `3.0`, a float, and a float can't be used as a list index. Use `//` when you need an int.

check.question: Which expression is True exactly when the int n is even?
check.explanation: % gives the remainder, and an even number leaves remainder 0 when divided by 2. n / 2 == 0 is only true when n is 0, and n // 2 == 0 is true for 0 and 1.

sections.title: Strings, slicing and f-strings
sections.body:
A sign-up form hands you `"  ada lovelace "`, with stray spaces and no capitals, and you want to show `Ada Lovelace`. Strings come with tools for exactly this kind of cleanup.

A **string** is a sequence of characters. Each character has an **index** starting at 0, and negative indexes count from the end, so `-1` is the last character. `len(s)` gives the number of characters.

A **slice** `s[start:stop:step]` takes characters from `start` up to but not including `stop`. Leave out `start` to begin at the first character, and leave out `stop` to run to the end. A step of `-1` walks backwards, so `s[::-1]` reverses a string. Slices are forgiving about positions past the end (`"abc"[1:99]` is `'bc'`), but plain indexing is not: `"abc"[5]` raises IndexError.

Strings are **immutable**: you can't change a character in place. String methods return a new string and leave the original alone:
- `s.upper()`, `s.lower()` and `s.title()` change case.
- `s.strip()` removes spaces and newlines from both ends.
- `s.replace("a", "b")` swaps every occurrence.
- `s.count("a")`, `s.startswith("http")` and `"lo" in s` answer questions about the text.

Because each method returns a string, you can chain them: `raw.strip().title()` strips first, then capitalizes each word of the result.

Join strings with `+` and repeat them with `*` (`"ab" * 3` is `'ababab'`). To mix text with numbers, use an **f-string**: write `f` before the opening quote and put any expression inside braces. After a colon you can add a format: `:.2f` for two decimal places, `:,` for thousands separators. f-strings convert values to text for you, so there is no need for `str()` inside them.
sections.code:
word = "recurse"
print(word[0])        # r
print(word[-1])       # e
print(word[1:4])      # ecu
print(word[::-1])     # esrucer
print(len(word))      # 7

raw = "  ada lovelace "
clean = raw.strip().title()
print(clean)                  # Ada Lovelace
print(len(raw), len(clean))   # 15 12  (raw itself is unchanged)

price = 3.5
print(f"{clean} owes ${price:.2f}")   # Ada Lovelace owes $3.50
print(f"{1234567:,}")                 # 1,234,567
sections.pitfall: Calling a method and ignoring the result. `name.upper()` on a line by itself changes nothing, because strings never change in place. Write `name = name.upper()`.

check.question: What does "python"[2:5] return?
check.explanation: Index 2 is t, and the slice stops before index 5, so you get t, h and o. 'thon' would need a stop of 6, and 'ytho' would start at index 1.

sections.title: Input, output and converting types
sections.body:
A tip calculator asks for the bill, the user types 40, and the program crashes with a TypeError. The reason is the single most common beginner bug in Python: `input()` always returns a string.

`input(prompt)` shows the prompt, waits for the user to press Enter, and returns exactly what they typed as a `str`, even when it's all digits. To do math with it, convert it first with `int()` or `float()`. Converting between types is called **casting**:
- `int("42")` is `42` and `float("2.5")` is `2.5`.
- `str(42)` is `'42'`, which you need when joining a number onto text with `+`.
- `int(3.9)` is `3`. Given a float, `int()` drops the decimal part instead of rounding.
- `int("3.5")` raises ValueError, because that text is not written as a whole number. Use `float()` for text that may contain a decimal point.
- `int("forty")` raises ValueError too. Later you will catch that with try and except; for now, know that bad input crashes the program at the cast.

A good habit is to convert on the same line you read: `age = int(input("Age? "))`. Every later line then works with a real number.

`print()` accepts any number of values, converts each to text, separates them with a space and ends with a newline. Change those with `sep=` and `end=`: `print("a", "b", sep="")` prints `ab`, and `end=""` keeps the next print on the same line. For anything more than a couple of values, an f-string is easier to read.

One note about the playground in this app: programs here can't read from the keyboard, so the activities store a value in a variable as if the user had typed it. In a real terminal, `input()` returns that same kind of string.
sections.code:
age = input("Age? ")             # the user types 20
print(type(age))                 # <class 'str'>
next_year = int(age) + 1
print("Next year:", next_year)   # Next year: 21
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")    # a-b-c
print("Loading", end="...")
print("done")                    # Loading...done
print(str(next_year) + "!")      # 21!
sections.pitfall: Converting too late. If you write `age = input()` and convert in only one place, every other use of age is still a string. Convert once, right where you read the value.

check.question: The user types 5 at n = input(). Which line prints 10?
check.explanation: n is the string '5', so int(n) * 2 is 10. n * 2, n + n and str(n) * 2 all give 55, because * repeats a string and + joins strings.

sections.title: Making decisions with if
sections.body:
A store gives free shipping on orders of $50 or more, but only on weekends. Rules like that become `if` statements.

An `if` statement runs its indented block only when its condition is true. Add `elif` (short for else if) branches for more cases and an optional `else` for everything left over. Python checks the conditions from top to bottom, runs only the **first** branch whose condition is true, and skips the rest. So order matters: put the strictest condition first, or an early branch will catch cases meant for a later one.

Conditions usually compare values, and every comparison produces a `bool`:
- `==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`.
- A single `=` assigns. Writing `if x = 5:` is a SyntaxError.
- `in` checks membership: `"@" in email`, `day in ("Sat", "Sun")`.
- String comparison is case sensitive: `"yes" == "Yes"` is False, so normalize with `.lower()` before comparing what a user typed.

Combine conditions with `and` (both must be true), `or` (at least one must be true) and `not` (flips True and False). Python also allows chained comparisons that read like math: `13 <= age <= 19` means `13 <= age and age <= 19`.

A classic trap is `if color == "red" or "blue":`. It reads like English, but Python groups it as `(color == "red") or "blue"`, and a non-empty string counts as true, so the condition is always true whatever color holds. Write `color == "red" or color == "blue"`, or better, `color in ("red", "blue")`.

You can nest an `if` inside another, but more than two levels quickly gets hard to follow. Often `and` or an `elif` says the same thing more flatly.
sections.tip: Order elif branches from the strictest condition to the loosest, or an early branch will catch everything.
sections.pitfall: `if color == "red" or "blue":` is always true. Each side of `or` must be a complete comparison, or use `in` with a tuple of options.

check.question: If score were 95 in this example, which branches would run?
choices: The A, B and C branches
check.explanation: 95 >= 90 is true, so grade becomes A and Python skips every remaining elif and the else, even though 95 >= 80 is also true.

sections.title: Loops: for, range and while
sections.body:
Printing a times table, adding up a column of prices, asking again until a password is right: all of these repeat the same steps, and loops do the repeating.

A `for` loop runs its block once for each item in a sequence, such as the characters of a string, the items of a list, or the numbers produced by `range()`. The loop variable takes each value in turn.

`range(stop)` counts from 0 up to but not including `stop`, so `range(5)` gives 0 to 4: five numbers. `range(start, stop)` chooses the first number, and `range(start, stop, step)` sets the jump between numbers. A negative step counts down: `range(5, 0, -1)` gives 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1.

Most loops follow the **accumulator** pattern: create a variable before the loop (a total of 0, a count of 0, an empty string), update it inside the loop, and use it after the loop. If you put the starting value inside the loop by mistake, it resets on every pass.

A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is true. It checks the condition before each pass, so it may run zero times. Something inside the loop must eventually make the condition false, or the loop runs forever. That's an **infinite loop**; press Ctrl+C in a terminal to stop it.

Use `for` when you know what you are looping over: each item, or n times. Use `while` when you loop until something changes and can't know in advance how many passes it takes, such as halving a number until it reaches 1, or asking again until the input is valid.
sections.code:
for n in range(2, 10, 3):
    print(n)                # 2, then 5, then 8

total = 0                   # the accumulator starts before the loop
for price in [4.5, 2.0, 3.5]:
    total += price          # same as total = total + price
print(total)                # 10.0

count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)            # 3, then 2, then 1
    count -= 1
print("liftoff")
sections.pitfall: Off-by-one errors: `range(1, 10)` stops at 9. To include 10, the stop must be 11.

check.question: What does list(range(5, 0, -2)) produce?
check.explanation: It starts at 5 and steps by -2, stopping before it reaches 0. So 5, 3 and 1 are produced; -1 is already past the stop value.

sections.title: Lists: storing many values
sections.body:
You have test scores for a whole class. Thirty separate variables would be miserable. One **list** holds them all, in order, and grows as you add more.

Write a list with square brackets: `scores = [77, 90, 85]`. Lists use the same indexes and slices as strings: `scores[0]` is the first item, `scores[-1]` the last and `scores[:2]` the first two. Unlike strings, lists are **mutable**, so you can change them in place:
- `scores.append(68)` adds one item to the end.
- `scores[1] = 88` replaces an item.
- `scores.remove(77)` deletes the first item equal to 77, and `scores.pop()` removes and returns the last item.
- `len(scores)` counts the items, and `x in scores` checks membership.
- `sum()`, `min()` and `max()` work on a list of numbers.

Asking for an index that doesn't exist raises IndexError. A list of 3 items has indexes 0, 1 and 2, so `scores[3]` fails. That off-by-one is the classic list bug.

To loop over a list, loop over the items directly with `for score in scores:`. You rarely need the index; when you do, the Loops and Functions topic shows `enumerate()`.

Sorting comes in two flavors, and mixing them up is a famous trap:
- `sorted(scores)` returns a new sorted list and leaves `scores` alone.
- `scores.sort()` sorts the list in place and returns `None`. So `scores = scores.sort()` throws your list away and leaves you holding `None`.

Both accept `reverse=True` for largest first. A list can hold any type, even other lists, though in practice a list usually holds one kind of thing.
sections.code:
scores = [77, 90, 85]
scores.append(68)
print(scores)                    # [77, 90, 85, 68]
print(len(scores), scores[-1])   # 4 68
print(85 in scores)              # True

best = max(scores)
average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print(f"Best {best}, average {average:.1f}")   # Best 90, average 80.0

ranked = sorted(scores, reverse=True)
print(ranked)                    # [90, 85, 77, 68]
print(scores)                    # [77, 90, 85, 68]  (unchanged)

for score in scores:
    if score < 70:
        print("Needs help:", score)   # Needs help: 68
sections.pitfall: `scores = scores.sort()` sets scores to None. Either call `scores.sort()` on its own line or write `scores = sorted(scores)`.

check.question: nums = [3, 1, 2]. Which line leaves nums holding [1, 2, 3]?
check.explanation: sort() sorts the list in place. nums = nums.sort() replaces the list with None. sorted(nums) builds a sorted copy but throws it away because the result isn't stored, and lists have no sorted() method.

sections.title: Functions, and reading error messages
sections.body:
You've written the same lines to convert Celsius to Fahrenheit in four places, and now you find a bug in them. A **function** lets you write those lines once, give them a name and use them anywhere.

`def` defines a function: a name, **parameters** in parentheses, a colon and an indented body. Calling the function with **arguments** runs the body with each parameter set to the matching argument. `return` sends a value back to the caller and ends the function immediately.

Return versus print is the key idea. `print()` shows text to a person. `return` hands a value to the code that called the function, so it can be stored, compared or passed on. A function without a `return` gives back `None`. Defining a function doesn't run it: nothing happens until you call it, and the `def` must have run before the line that calls it.

When something goes wrong, Python prints a **traceback**. Read it from the bottom up:
- The last line names the error type and gives a message.
- Just above it is the line of code that failed, and above that, `File ..., line N` says where it is. Python 3.11 and later also underline the exact part of the line that failed.
- When functions are involved there is one File entry per call, from your top-level code at the top down to the line that actually failed at the bottom.

In the example, the crash is on line 2 inside `fahrenheit`, but the real mistake is on line 12, which passes the string `"20"`. `"20" * 9` repeats the text instead of multiplying, and dividing text by 5 is a TypeError. Always ask where the bad value came from.

The errors you'll meet most:
- `SyntaxError` and `IndentationError`: the code isn't valid Python. Nothing runs.
- `NameError`: a name that doesn't exist yet, usually a typo.
- `TypeError`: the wrong type for an operation, such as `"3" + 4`, or the wrong number of arguments.
- `ValueError`: the right type with a bad value, such as `int("abc")`.
- `IndexError`: an index past the end of a list or string.
sections.code:
def fahrenheit(celsius):
    return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32


def show(celsius):
    print(f"{celsius} C is {fahrenheit(celsius)} F")


show(100)          # 100 C is 212.0 F
result = show(0)   # 0 C is 32.0 F
print(result)      # None, because show prints but returns nothing
show("20")         # crashes with this traceback:

# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "temps.py", line 12, in <module>
#     show("20")
#   File "temps.py", line 6, in show
#     print(f"{celsius} C is {fahrenheit(celsius)} F")
#   File "temps.py", line 2, in fahrenheit
#     return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
# TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'str' and 'int'
sections.tip: Professional developers read tracebacks all day. The skill is reading them calmly: error type, failing line, then the value that was wrong.
sections.pitfall: Printing inside a function when the caller needs the value. If a function prints its answer instead of returning it, the caller gets None, and the crash shows up far away from the real mistake.

check.question: A function prints its result but has no return statement. What does result = f() store in result?
choices: Nothing: the line raises an error
check.explanation: Every function call produces a value, and a function that finishes without return produces None. The printed text went to the screen, not to the caller.

keyTerms.definition: The interactive Python prompt (>>>) that reads a line, runs it, prints the result and waits for the next one.
A file of Python code, run with a command such as python3 file.py, that executes from top to bottom.
The kind of a value, such as int, float, str or bool, which decides what you can do with it.
The // operator: divide and round down to a whole number.
The % operator: the remainder after division, as in 7 % 3 == 1.
A piece of a sequence written s[start:stop:step]; the stop position is not included.
A string literal prefixed with f whose {expressions} are replaced by their values.
Converting a value to another type, for example int("42") or str(42).
An ordered, mutable collection written with square brackets, such as [77, 90, 85].
A variable set before a loop and updated on each pass, such as a running total.
The value a function hands back to its caller with return; None if there is no return.
The error report Python prints when a program crashes; read it from the bottom up.

summary: Run scripts with python3 file.py and use the REPL to try ideas; only the REPL echoes values without print.
/ always gives a float, // rounds down and % gives the remainder.
Indexes start at 0, slices stop before their stop index, and string methods return new strings.
input() always returns a string, so cast with int() or float() before doing math.
Only the first true branch of an if chain runs, range() excludes its stop value, and list.sort() returns None.
Functions hand values back with return; read tracebacks from the bottom up and ask where the bad value came from.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never programmed why int(input()) is needed before adding 1 to what the user typed, and how you would use the error message to find the problem if you forgot it.

questions.question: A script has five lines. Line 3 uses a variable name that was never assigned. What happens when you run it?
choices: Python skips line 3 and runs lines 4 and 5
Lines 1 and 2 run, then the program stops at line 3 with a NameError
Nothing runs, because Python checks every name before starting
All five lines run and the error is reported at the end
questions.explanation: Python executes lines in order and only discovers the missing name when it reaches line 3, so lines 1 and 2 have already run. Python checks syntax before starting, but not whether names exist, so the program does start.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
x = 5
x = x + 2
x = x * 10
print(x)
questions.explanation: Each line runs in order. x becomes 7, then 7 * 10 = 70. The right side is evaluated with the current value of x before the new value is stored.

questions.question: This script crashes on its first line. Why?
choices: print() can only display quoted strings, not variables
message is a reserved word in Python
message is used before the line that assigns it, so Python raises NameError
Variables must be declared with a type before use
questions.explanation: Python runs top to bottom, so when line 1 runs, message doesn't exist yet. Swap the two lines. Python never needs type declarations, and print() can show any variable.

questions.question: What does "recurse"[-3:] return?
questions.explanation: -3 is the third character from the end, 'r', and leaving out stop runs to the end, giving 'rse'. 'rec' would be [:3], the first three characters.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The slice starts at index 1 and takes every second character: indexes 1, 3 and 5, which are all 'a'. Leaving out stop means it runs to the end of the string.

questions.question: Complete the f-string so it prints Total: 4.50
questions.explanation: In an f-string the format goes after a colon, and .2f means two digits after the decimal point. :2f sets a minimum width of 2 instead and prints 4.500000. The other two options are syntax errors.

questions.question: This code should print Jane. What is wrong?
choices: Strings are immutable, so name[0] can't be assigned; build a new string such as "J" + name[1:]
The first character of a string is at index 1, not 0
Single characters must be written with single quotes
name must be converted with str() before indexing
questions.explanation: Python raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. Strings can't change in place, so create a new one; name.capitalize() also works. Index 0 is valid and refers to the first character.

questions.explanation: + joins two strings, giving '34', and adds two ints, giving 7. print separates its two values with a space. There is no TypeError because each + has the same type on both sides.

questions.question: The user types 21. Why does this crash?
choices: if statements can't compare against a number literal
age is the string '21', and comparing a string with an int raises TypeError; use int(input(...))
input() returns None until the user presses Enter twice
questions.explanation: input() always returns a string, and Python refuses to order a str against an int, so it raises TypeError. Convert first: age = int(input("Age? ")). Parentheses around a condition are optional.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: int("12") is 12. int(3.9) drops the decimal part instead of rounding, giving 3. So the total is 15, not 16.

questions.question: What happens when Python runs int("3.5")?
questions.explanation: int() only parses text that looks like a whole number, and '3.5' doesn't, so it raises ValueError. int(3.5) with a float works and returns 3; for the string, use int(float("3.5")).

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Python runs only the first branch whose condition is true. 25 > 10 is checked first, so it prints warm and skips the elif, even though 25 > 20 is also true. Checking temp > 20 first would fix the order.
questions.concept: only the first true branch runs

questions.question: Complete the condition so it prints teen only for ages 13 to 19.
questions.explanation: Both conditions must be true, which is what and means. With or, every age passes, because every number is either at least 13 or at most 19. && is not Python syntax. 13 <= age <= 19 would also work.

questions.question: Complete the condition so it checks whether guess equals secret.
questions.code:
secret = 7
guess = 7
if guess _____ secret:
    print("correct")
questions.explanation: == compares two values. A single = assigns, and inside an if condition it is a SyntaxError. === exists in JavaScript, not Python.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total += n
print(total)
questions.explanation: range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3 and 4 and stops before 5, so the total is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. If you got 15, you included the stop value.

questions.question: This program never prints done. What is wrong?
choices: while loops can't use the < operator
print(count) must come after the loop
count should start at 1 instead of 0
count never changes, so count < 3 stays true forever; add count += 1 inside the loop
questions.explanation: The loop prints 0 over and over because nothing updates count. Adding count += 1 inside the loop makes the condition false after three passes. Starting at 1 would still loop forever.

questions.question: When would you choose a for loop, and when a while loop?
questions.answer: Use a for loop when you know what you are iterating over, such as a list, a string or range(n). Use a while loop when you repeat until a condition changes and can't know the number of passes in advance, such as asking again until the input is valid.
questions.explanation: A for loop steps through the items for you. A while loop relies on you to update its condition, which is why forgetting that update causes an infinite loop.

questions.question: In the REPL, typing 2 + 3 shows 5. What does a script containing only the line 2 + 3 show when you run it?
choices: Nothing: a script only shows what you print
A SyntaxError, because the line has no print
questions.explanation: The REPL echoes the value of every expression you type, but a script calculates 2 + 3 and throws the result away. A bare expression is valid Python, so there's no error. In scripts, use print(2 + 3).

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: // and * have the same precedence and run left to right: 17 // 5 is 3, and 3 * 5 is 15. % also binds tighter than +, so 17 % 5 is 2, and 15 + 2 is 17. This always holds: (n // d) * d + n % d gives back n.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
n = 10
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)
questions.explanation: n goes 10, 5, 2, 1. That is three passes; after the third, n is 1 and n > 1 is false, so the loop stops. Writing down n and steps after each pass is the reliable way to trace a while loop.

questions.question: This should print all three scores. It prints 85 and 77, then crashes with IndexError. Why?
choices: len(scores) is 2, because counting starts at 0
range() can't be combined with len()
print() can't show list items inside a loop
Indexes run 0 to 2, so the loop skips scores[0] and then asks for scores[3]; loop with for score in scores
questions.explanation: range(1, 4) gives 1, 2 and 3. Index 1 and 2 print 85 and 77, and index 3 doesn't exist in a 3-item list. len(scores) is 3. Looping over the items directly avoids index bugs entirely.

questions.question: Why does this raise TypeError?
choices: greet requires one argument and is called with none: greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'name'
return can't be combined with string concatenation
Functions must be defined after the line that calls them
name is a reserved word in Python
questions.explanation: Each parameter without a default needs an argument. Call greet("Ada"). The def does come first here, which is correct: a function must be defined before the line that calls it runs.

questions.question: Match each line of code to the error it raises.
questions.explanation: SyntaxError means the code isn't valid Python. NameError is an unknown name. TypeError is the wrong type for an operation. ValueError is the right type with a bad value. IndexError is a position past the end.

questions.question: Put these steps for fixing a crash from its traceback in order.
items: Read the last line for the error type and message
Find the File entry just above it to get the line that failed
Look at the values used on that line and spot the one that is wrong
Trace back to where that value came from and fix it there
Run the program again to confirm the fix
questions.explanation: Start from the bottom of the traceback: the error and the failing line. The wrong value often comes from somewhere else, such as a caller passing a string, so fix it at its source and rerun.

questions.question: Read this traceback. On which line of report.py was the error actually raised? Type the number.
questions.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "report.py", line 7, in <module>
    print(average(scores))
          ~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
  File "report.py", line 3, in average
    return total / len(values)
           ~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
questions.explanation: The bottom File entry is where the error was raised: line 3, inside average. Line 7 is the call that led there. The message explains why: values was an empty list, so len(values) was 0. The fix is to guard against an empty list, in average or in the caller.
